title: TOWARD RESILIENT DAMLESS WATER INTAKE SYSTEMS: HYDRAULIC AND SEDIMENT CONTROL STRATEGIES FROM THE AMU DARYA

TOWARD RESILIENT DAMLESS WATER INTAKE SYSTEMS: HYDRAULIC AND SEDIMENT CONTROL STRATEGIES FROM THE AMU DARYA

Journal: Water Conservation and Management (WCM)
Author: Azizali Kurbanov, Ruslan Baimanov, Javlonbek Suyunov, Bekhzod Norkulov, Norkobul Rakhmatov, Ikboloy Salimbaeva

ABSTRACT

This article presents research results and operational experience related to large damless water intakes on the Amu Darya River. The study provides a scientific assessment of multifactor channel processes typical of rivers flowing through easily erodible soils in Central Asia. Key phenomena affecting water intake operation are analyzed, including bank erosion, channel migration, the formation of mid-channel bars, development of deigish erosion features, and intensive sediment transport that leads to siltation and operational instability of intake structures. Numerical simulations were performed to evaluate hydraulic and morphodynamic processes in the intake zone. The results show that in order to ensure reliable water withdrawal during low-water periods, trenches with lengths of 500-800 m should be constructed near the intake. Modeling results indicate that the overall flow pattern in the intake zone remains practically unchanged, while flow velocities within the trench become significantly lower than in the main river channel. As a result, a considerable portion of transported sediments is deposited in the trench, reducing sediment inflow into the channel. The study also demonstrates that reducing the channel width using semi-dikes (spurs) increases local flow depth and velocity at the intake, improving hydraulic conditions for stable water diversion. In addition, installing an auxiliary sill at the intake entrance increases the upstream water level by approximately 0.15-0.25 m during low-flow conditions while decreasing near-bed velocities and partially protecting the intake from sediment inflow. Increased velocities over the sill also promote downstream sediment transport, which contributes to lowering the turbidity of water entering the channel. The novelty of this study lies in the integrated use of field observations and two-dimensional numerical modeling to quantitatively evaluate the influence of trenches, flow-guiding spurs, and intake sills on sediment transport, flow velocity, and water levels at large damless water intakes in morphodynamically active river channels. The obtained results provide practical recommendations for improving the reliability and operational efficiency of damless water intakes and can be applied to the design and operation of the Qosh Tepa Channel.
